job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and two younger sisters in Redmond Heights, above the family grocery. I'm up before dawn for prayer, then I help unload the morning delivery before my applications. I spend the day coding, mostly a stock app for Dad's shop, and sending out applications. In the evening I help my sisters with homework. I use an AI assistant all day for code and for writing, and I'm always testing the newest tools.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What was your degree, and what did you do for your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Information systems at Lowell University. My final project was an inventory app for my uncle's shop that predicted what to reorder, and it cut his wasted stock by about a fifth. My internship was twelve weeks at a logistics software company, fixing small bugs and writing tests. I'm looking for a developer job, but honestly I'd also love to build my own product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and not a miracle. I'd tell customers at the shop that it won't take their jobs, and I'd keep showing them how a small tool saves them time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job market is what bothers me, not AI. There are plenty of developer jobs near Redmond Heights, but a few hundred graduates apply to each one, and I've been through six interview rounds without an offer. I'm patient, but I do count the weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and I'd turn the shop app into a product other grocers can use, with a small monthly price. I'd contribute to an open-source project to show my code in public. And I'd ask my internship boss, Ms Ortega, for a recommendation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Money isn't a problem, and I enjoy building. I'm just impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said six interview rounds without an offer. What do you take from that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm good enough to get in the room and not yet good enough to be the first choice. I've started asking for feedback after each one, and two said my communication was my weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you work on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I explain code to my sisters. If a thirteen-year-old understands my idea, an interviewer will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for people who build things. I'd tell friends and relatives to pick up the tools now, and I'd tell the mosque youth group we should run a free workshop on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm not too worried about myself. The coding tasks that juniors get are exactly what goes first, but I'm already using the tools every day, so I'd offer fast, checked work. What worries me is that fewer firms will hire juniors at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for roles where I'd supervise AI-written code, or at small firms that need a generalist. I'd also build more of my own product and offer it to local shops. And I'd run that workshop at the mosque on Fridays, since it builds contacts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It feels like a moving market, and I can move with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer firms will hire juniors. What does that mean for your product idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it more important. If the market won't hire me, I'd rather be paid by shops that use my tool. A small steady income from twenty grocers beats waiting on one HR department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Imran, who works in a call centre. His job is exactly on that list, and he doesn't believe it. I'd sit him down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is incredibly fast, but I'd say publicly that we should move quickly and sensibly, not panic, and that governments must back small businesses and families. I'd say we need clear rules fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the first time I feel properly anxious. Software is thinking work, so my own field is in the first wave. I'm ahead of most on the tools, but when a machine does the whole job, being good with tools isn't a job anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch my product to as many shops as I can in the next six months, so I'd have a business and not just a CV. I'd save every spare pound, and I'd help my parents prepare the shop for fewer customers. I'd also look at hands-on supply and logistics work, which lasts until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not frozen, I'm busy, but there's a stone in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being good with tools isn't a job anymore. What is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owning something, I think. Whoever owns the tool, the shop or the customer relationship still earns, and whoever sells hours of thinking work doesn't. I'd want to be on the owning side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sisters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay in school but learn how to run a small business and how to deal with people. And keep an eye on how Dad runs the shop, because that's a real education.

Governments must back small businesses and families with clear rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a window and I'd say people should use it to build something of their own. I'd tell my friends to pick a niche and own it, and I'd tell the mosque group to learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a good deal. I could get a developer job for two years, learn how a real company runs, and have a product ready by 2031. The risk is that the market for coders thins before I get my foot in the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any developer job that pays, spend evenings on my product and save half my pay. I'd also keep helping the shop modernise, with a stock system, online ordering and delivery routes. And I'd think about starting a small company with my cousin around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It's a race, and I like a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a race. Who are you racing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly myself. Other graduates are fast, but I'm not trying to beat other graduates, I'm trying to be useful before the market decides I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your first employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty and a chance to build something that ships. I'd also want them to let me finish my own side product in my own time, without trying to own it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of runway. I'd say we should use it to build skills, businesses and savings, and that governments should keep the rules simple for small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly exciting. By 2036 I'd be 33, maybe running a small company that serves grocers and other family businesses. I'd still worry about people who aren't paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by working a couple of years, then go full-time on the product. I'd keep up with the tools every week. I'd marry at some point, buy a flat above a shop of our own, and help my sisters through university, because that's part of what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ambitious. This is the picture where I get to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said help your sisters through university. Why is that part of your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the eldest and my parents did the same for me. It's what we do, and I'd rather pay for my sisters' degrees than for a flash car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop could be squeezed by big chains using the same technology. I'd need to be sure my tool keeps small grocers ahead. If I can't do that, I'd go to the chains myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, but only just. I like risk, and I'd probably be fine, but my parents' shop and my sisters' futures depend on a lot of people having money to spend. If those people are out of work, the shop suffers. What would help is clear rules and a path for small business owners, and strong families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That people see my generation as lazy with technology. I read the new tools every week. I just want a fair chance to use them.

headlineQuote: I read the new tools every week. I just want a fair chance to use them.
portrait: Bilal is a **23-year-old** information systems graduate living above his family's grocery, still without a first offer after several months.
He is **traditional**, faithful and pro-market, and he wants to build his own product while helping the family shop and his sisters.
He uses **AI tools** every day and tests new ones weekly, so he moves early and takes risks.
His mood is **calm** or uneasy until the 2028 world, where he turns anxious mainly about the shop and his sisters.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, only because the family shop depends on customers who would have money.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear rules** and a path for small business owners, and strong **families**.
